title: The SBA Loan Process: A Step-by-Step Guide From Prequalification to Funding
summary: You apply for an SBA loan through an approved lender, not the SBA. Learn each step from prequalification to funding, plus documents, timelines, and costs.
body_markdown:
### How the SBA loan process works


The SBA loan process is how a small business applies for a loan through an SBA-approved lender, not through the SBA itself. The lender underwrites the loan and submits it to the U.S. Small Business Administration for a partial guarantee. The core stages run in order: choose a program, check eligibility, find a lender, gather documents, apply, complete underwriting, get SBA authorization, and close.


The U.S. Small Business Administration's[SBA 7(a) loan overview](https://www.sba.gov/loans/7a-loans/) puts it plainly: you always work directly with your lender, not with SBA. SBA guarantees the lender, not the borrower.


Per the SBA's 7(a) loan types page, most 7(a) programs guarantee up to 85% at $150,000 or less and 75% above. The same U.S. Small Business Administration page lists a 50% guarantee for SBA Express loans.


According to the U.S. Small Business Administration's[SBA fiscal 2025 results](https://legacy.sba.gov/article/2025/09/30/trump-sba-delivers-record-capital-small-businesses-fy25) , the agency guaranteed 84,400 7(a) and 504 loans for $44.8 billion. Each of those loans ran through a lender, which makes the SBA loan process a lender workflow at its core. How well a lender runs intake, document collection, and decisions shapes most of what you experience as a borrower.


This guide reflects SBA rules as of October 2026. Program limits, fees, and procedures change each fiscal year, so confirm current terms with your lender.


‍


### Choose the right SBA loan program


SBA offers several loan programs, and each fits a different use of funds. Match your purpose to the right program first—it saves time with every lender you talk to.


Program Maximum amount SBA guarantee Best fit Where you apply


Standard 7(a) $5 million Up to 85% (≤$150K); up to 75% above General business purposes, including changes of ownership SBA-approved lenders


SBA Express $500,000 50% Smaller financing needs SBA-approved lenders


504 $5.5 million per SBA's 504 page — Fixed-rate financing for fixed assets; not working capital or inventory Certified Development Companies (CDCs)


Microloan $50,000 (average about $13,000) — Small loans with rates generally between 8% and 13% Nonprofit intermediary lenders


The 504 program works differently from 7(a). The U.S. Small Business Administration's[SBA 504 loan program](https://www.sba.gov/loans/504-loans/) page states that 504 loans are available exclusively through Certified Development Companies (CDCs).


The guarantee levels and Express terms in the table come from the U.S. Small Business Administration's 7(a) loan types page. That page caps SBA Express loans at $500,000 with a 50% guarantee.


Microloans are the smallest option. The U.S. Small Business Administration's[SBA microloan program](https://www.sba.gov/loans/microloans/) provides loans up to $50,000 through nonprofit community-based intermediaries, with an average of about $13,000. Rates vary by intermediary, generally between 8% and 13%, and proceeds can't pay existing debts or buy real estate.


**New in 2026:** Since July 4, 2026, borrowers can stack both programs. The U.S. Small Business Administration announced a[$10M combined SBA limit](https://legacy.sba.gov/article/2026/07/07/small-businesses-now-eligible-10-million-sba-financing) that lets borrowers combine 7(a) and 504 loans. That means up to $5 million through each program, up from a previous cumulative limit of $5 million.


The individual 7(a) maximum stays at $5 million. 7(a) also covers changes of ownership, so buyers can use it to purchase an existing business. Brokers handling these deals can follow a dedicated[business acquisition SBA workflow](https://www.lendflow.com/post/business-acquisition-sba-loans-for-brokers) .


SBA loans also sit alongside other products. Lendflow supports SBA loans together with term loans, lines of credit, equipment financing, and other[Lendflow-supported financing types](https://www.lendflow.com/customers/financing-types) .


‍


### Confirm you meet SBA eligibility requirements


Eligibility is the first gate in the SBA loan process. According to the U.S. Small Business Administration's 7(a) page, these are the baseline 7(a) criteria, and lenders add their own credit standards on top.


- **Operate for profit:** The business must be a for-profit company.
- **Be small:** The business must meet size requirements listed in the U.S. Small Business Administration's[SBA size standards tool](https://www.sba.gov/size-standards/) .
- **Lack reasonable credit elsewhere:** You must be unable to get the credit on reasonable terms from non-government sources.
- **Show ability to repay:** You must be creditworthy and demonstrate a reasonable ability to repay the loan.


Lenders set their own criteria on top of SBA's list, including any minimum credit score. They may also require an owner equity contribution, so ask about it early.


Lenders review business credit as well as personal credit. Learn[what's on a business credit report](https://www.lendflow.com/post/what-shows-up-on-a-business-credit-report) before you apply so nothing surprises you.


Eligibility checks are moving earlier in the process. Lenders using modern intake tools can screen fit automatically with enriched business data—flagging issues before you spend hours on a full application.


‍


### Find and choose an SBA-approved lender


The fastest way to find interested lenders is SBA's matching service. With the U.S. Small Business Administration's[SBA Lender Match tool](https://www.sba.gov/loans/lender-match/) , you get a summary of interested lenders two business days after you submit a request. More than 800 lenders participate across all 50 states and U.S. territories.


Lender Match is not an application. Using it doesn't guarantee a match or a loan offer. Compare the lenders who respond on these points:


- **SBA lending volume:** Lenders that close SBA loans regularly know the forms and review steps.
- **Industry experience:** A lender that knows your industry reads your financials in context.
- **Digital application tools:** Online applications and document uploads cut back-and-forth.
- **Communication:** Clear status updates keep you from guessing where your file stands.


For lenders and brokers, borrower experience is a real differentiator. Lendflow's Borrower Platform gives borrowers one unified place to apply and track progress. AI communications tools save lenders hours on status updates.


‍


### Gather the documents lenders require


SBA lending is document-intensive—borrowers may need financial statements, tax returns, bank statements, and ownership information before a lender can decide. The table lists typical lender requests; the SBA forms covered here are SBA Form 1919 and SBA Form 413. Confirm the exact list and date requirements with your lender.


Typical lender request What it shows Notes


SBA Form 1919 Borrower information and eligibility SBA form; required for every standard 7(a) loan


Personal financial statement (SBA Form 413) Owner assets, liabilities, and net worth SBA form; lender confirms which owners complete one


Business tax returns Historical business income Lender sets the number of years


Personal tax returns Owner income Lender confirms which owners file


Financial statements Profitability and financial position Profit and loss statement and balance sheet


Business bank statements Cash flow and balances Lender sets the number of months


Ownership information Who owns the business and in what share Include organizational documents


Business plan and projections How you'll use funds and repay Most important for newer businesses


Licenses and legal documents Authority to operate Leases, contracts, and registrations


Collateral documentation Assets you may pledge Needed if your lender requires collateral


Acquisition documents Deal terms and the target business's finances Changes of ownership only


The two SBA forms have defined roles. The U.S. Small Business Administration's[SBA Form 1919](https://www.sba.gov/document/sba-form-1919-borrower-information-form) is completed by the business applying for a 7(a) loan and submitted to the lender. The U.S. Small Business Administration uses[SBA Form 413](https://www.sba.gov/document/sba-form-413-personal-financial-statement) to assess repayment ability and creditworthiness of 7(a) and 504 applicants.


Missing or outdated documents can lead to follow-up requests. On the lender side, AI document analysis catches issues at upload, not later in underwriting. Lendflow's[Doc Analyzer Agent](https://www.lendflow.com/solutions/doc-analyzer) reviews documents as they arrive, so teams spend less time on manual checks.


‍


### Walk through the SBA loan application step by step


Once you've picked a program and a lender, the SBA loan application process follows five steps. Each step has a borrower task and a lender task.


Each step can also move faster with the right tools. Here's what happens at each stage and where automation helps.


#### Step 1: Prequalify


**42% faster speed to funding:** That's the average for pre-qualified offers hosted on Lendflow. Prequalification is an early fit check, not an approval.


Many lenders start with prequalification, where you share basic information about your business and how much you need. To learn how credit checks differ, read[soft pull vs. hard pull](https://www.lendflow.com/post/soft-pull-vs-hard-pull) before you start.


#### Step 2: Submit the full application


Next, you complete the lender's application, the required SBA forms, and your document package. A complete package up front means fewer follow-up requests later.


Lenders with a unified borrower portal let you apply, upload documents, and track status in one place. Skip scattered email threads—use one portal to keep every document and update together.


#### Step 3: Lender underwriting


The lender reviews your credit, cash flow, repayment ability, and collateral. Expect follow-up questions, and answer them quickly to keep your file moving.


Underwriting moves faster when lenders work from current information. Real-time data, live credit signals, and decision workflows replace manual re-keying and disconnected review steps.


#### Step 4: SBA authorization


After the lender approves your loan, it submits the loan to SBA for the guarantee. Per the SBA's 7(a) loan types page, SBA's published review turnaround is 5–10 business days for standard 7(a) loans and 2–10 for 7(a) Small loans.


#### Step 5: Closing and funding


At closing, you sign the loan documents and satisfy any closing conditions your lender sets. The lender then disburses the funds.


‍


### How long the SBA loan process takes


SBA's published review turnaround covers only SBA's step; total time to funding varies by lender and loan type. The U.S. Small Business Administration lists its turnaround on the[SBA 7(a) loan types](https://www.sba.gov/partners/lenders/7a-loan-program/types-7a-loans) page. Standard 7(a) loans take 5–10 business days, and 7(a) Small loans take 2–10 business days.


That same SBA page notes that SBA Form 1919 is required for every standard 7(a) loan. It's also the source for this guide's guarantee levels, Express terms, and $50,000 collateral rule.


Total time to funding varies by lender and loan type. The rest of the timeline depends on steps such as document collection, follow-up requests, and lender underwriting.


Stage Who acts What drives the timeline


1. Prequalify Borrower and lender How quickly you share basic business information


2. Application and documents Borrower How complete your document package is


3. Underwriting Lender Follow-up requests and your response time


4. SBA authorization SBA 5–10 business days for Standard 7(a); 2–10 for 7(a) Small


5. Closing and funding Borrower and lender Closing conditions and signatures


You control more of the SBA loan timeline than you might expect. These three habits cut the most delay:


- **Prepare documents early:** Assemble tax returns, financial statements, and Form 1919 before you apply.
- **Respond fast:** Answer lender questions the same day when you can.
- **Choose a lender with digital workflows:** Online uploads and status tracking remove email back-and-forth.


**80% smaller teams:** Lendflow's embedded finance customers operate with 80% smaller teams while converting similar funding volumes. For lenders, operational overhead is the real timeline driver. Read more on[scaling SBA deal flow](https://www.lendflow.com/post/how-sba-lenders-can-grow-deal-flow-without-adding-operational-overhead) without adding headcount.

### SBA loan costs: rates, fees, and collateral


In the SBA loan process, costs include interest, an upfront guarantee fee, and any collateral your lender requires. The figures below apply as of October 2026, and SBA revisits fees each fiscal year.


**Interest rates:** You negotiate the rate with your lender, subject to SBA maximums. For variable-rate 7(a) loans, federal regulations published on eCFR as[13 CFR 120.214 rate limits](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/section-120.214) cap the rate at a base rate plus a spread. The base rate is the prime rate or SBA's optional peg rate.


- **$50,000 or less:** Base rate plus 6.5%.
- **$50,001 to $250,000:** Base rate plus 6.0%.
- **$250,001 to $350,000:** Base rate plus 4.5%.
- **Greater than $350,000:** Base rate plus 3.0%.


**Guarantee fees:** Tiers are per SBA's FY2027 notice, as summarized by the National Association of Government Guaranteed Lenders (NAGGL) in its[SBA FY2027 fee notice](https://www.naggl.org/sba-issues-notices-announcing-fy-2027-7a-and-504-loan-program-fees/) post. SBA's FY2027 7(a) fee notice covers 7(a) loans approved October 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027, with maturities over 12 months.


- **$150,000 or less:** 2% of the guaranteed portion.
- **$150,001 to $700,000:** 3% of the guaranteed portion.
- **$700,001 to $5 million:** 3.5% of the guaranteed portion up to $1 million, plus 3.75% of the portion above $1 million.


The fee is a percentage of the guaranteed portion, not the full loan amount. A 0% fee applies to certain loans of $700,000 or less, including loans to manufacturers. Fees change each fiscal year, so confirm current fees with your lender.


**Collateral and down payment:** The SBA's 7(a) loan types page states that SBA does not require collateral on 7(a) Small loans of $50,000 or less. The same U.S. Small Business Administration page says Express lenders aren't required to take collateral up to $50,000.


No collateral requirement doesn't mean no personal guarantee. Under federal regulations published on eCFR as[13 CFR 120.160 guarantees](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/section-120.160) , holders of at least 20% ownership generally must guarantee the loan.


Above $50,000, lender policy applies, so ask your lender what it requires. Ask early about any owner equity contribution, often called a down payment, and how much you'll need.


‍


### What to do if your SBA application is declined


A decline isn't the end of the SBA loan process. The Federal Reserve Banks'[Small Business Credit Survey report](https://www.fedsmallbusiness.org/reports/survey/2026/2026-report-on-employer-firms) found that 42% of employer-firm applicants received the full amount of financing they sought. Another 36% received some or most, and 22% received none.


Those survey figures cover all financing types, not SBA loans specifically. Still, they show partial and full declines are a normal part of borrowing. Here's how to respond:


- **Ask for the reasons:** Ask the lender for the specific reasons for the decision.
- **Strengthen credit and cash flow:** Pay down balances, correct report errors, and build cash reserves before reapplying.
- **Try another SBA lender:** Credit criteria vary by lender, so a different lender may view your file differently.
- **Consider alternative financing:** Term loans, lines of credit, or equipment financing may fit while you build toward an SBA loan.


For lenders and brokers, a decline doesn't have to mean a lost borrower. Second-look networks route declined applicants to other lenders that may approve them. Lendflow's[Second Look Marketplace](https://www.lendflow.com/solutions/second-look-marketplace) and decline waterfalls help ensure no deal leaves money on the table.

### FAQs


#### How long is the process for an SBA loan?


The SBA's 7(a) loan types page lists 5–10 business days of SBA review for standard 7(a) loans and 2–10 for 7(a) Small loans. Total time to funding varies by lender, loan type, and how quickly you supply documents.


#### What is the easiest SBA loan to get approved for?


SBA microloans go up to $50,000 (about $13,000 on average) through nonprofit intermediaries. SBA requires no collateral on 7(a) Small loans of $50,000 or less, but approval ultimately depends on the lender's criteria.


#### What documents do I need to apply for an SBA loan?


Lenders typically request SBA Form 1919, SBA Form 413 (personal financial statement), financial statements, business and personal tax returns, and a business plan. Your lender confirms the exact list and date requirements.


#### What are the eligibility requirements for an SBA loan?


For 7(a) loans, your business must operate for profit and be small under SBA size requirements. You must also be creditworthy with a reasonable ability to repay and unable to get credit on reasonable terms elsewhere.


#### Can I get an SBA loan without collateral?


Per the SBA's 7(a) loan types page, SBA doesn't require collateral on 7(a) Small loans of $50,000 or less. Above that amount, your lender's collateral policy applies.


#### How do I find an SBA-approved lender?


Use SBA's Lender Match, which sends you a summary of interested lenders about two business days after you submit a request.


#### What is the difference between an SBA 7(a) and 504 loan?


A 7(a) loan covers general business purposes up to $5 million and comes from SBA-approved lenders. A 504 loan finances fixed assets through Certified Development Companies and can't be used for working capital or inventory.
